Rendered through stateOf that came out as '✓ ran clean' with 'No commits in range to sweep' underneath — the tick asserting a measurement for work that did not happen, and the sub-line arguing with the label above it. The same lie, told the other way round.

New sixth state, nothing_scanned: a SUCCEEDED run that still carries an error string. The only writer of that shape is scan-processor's zero-work path. Checked after failed and partial so it can never swallow the more serious reading.

tickets.title: A finding link resolves against the recipient's filters, not the sender's
acceptance: A link to a finding opens it whatever the recipient's filters are
notes: W16-16 put the open finding in the URL, and the filters are still component state — so a link to a dismissed finding, opened by someone whose Status filter is the default 'open', finds nothing in the list. It now says so ('not in the current view') instead of landing silently, which is the honest half.

Two ways to finish it, and they are not exclusive: serialize the filters into the URL alongside ?finding= (which FR-WEB-2 arguably already asks for), and/or add GET /findings/:id so the panel can fetch a finding the list does not contain. The endpoint does not exist — /findings/:id/history does, which is the near miss that makes it look like it should.

tickets.title: owasp_web and owasp_llm have no runner, so nothing can start them
acceptance: An OWASP checklist pass runs end to end from the worker
The catalogue lists both as startable, or says why they are not
notes: Split out of W16-11 after I mis-scoped that ticket. runOwaspChecklist and both checklists exist and are tested; no worker runner calls either, and neither has a catalogue entry, so both read 'not in this build' on the Security tab — truthfully.

Both are LLM-backed and need an AnalysisGateway, which W16-19 now resolves per workspace. They also need a DIFF rather than a snapshot (chunkDiff over changed files), so they do not fit the weekly snapshot runners that anti_slop and semgrep share — that is the design question this ticket has to answer, not just wiring.
dependency_cve is the third of the same shape: runDependencyScan exists with no caller. Catalogued but not startable, and disabled by default until something calls it.

DONE 2026-08-28. Both checklists wired as MANUAL-ONLY runners over the newest ingested commit's DIFF — not the weekly snapshot the other scanners share, because chunkDiff reviews changed files and their own defaults say a human starts them ('costly per run'). Catalogued with triggers ['manual'] and left disabled by default, so nothing runs a model over every repo without being asked.

Verified against the REAL local model, and it found two more bugs on the way: the fake forge served commit files with NO `patch` field at all, and its commit-detail route regex `[0-9a-z]+` rejected the seeder's shas (`payments-c1`) so it 404'd for every commit in the demo. Both fixed. That second one also means the secrets STREAM scanner — the one meant to catch a credential within 60s of a webhook — had never been handed a line of source against this fake.

The final run reached the model host and stopped there: LM Studio refused to load the model for 'insufficient system resources' on this machine. The wiring is proven end to end (provider -> diff -> chunker -> gateway -> host) and the model's own answer is NOT verified. The error reaches the screen verbatim, which is the behaviour wanted.

MODEL ANSWER NOW VERIFIED (2026-08-28, Brad supplied a second host). Against qwen3.8-27b-mlx-textonly on http://192.168.13.179:1234/v1 the checklist ran for ~3 minutes and completed: scan_run succeeded, scannerVersion owasp-web.v1, partial false, 0 findings. So the earlier 'reached the host and stopped' caveat is closed — the local machine was simply out of memory.

tickets.title: Full-suite runs fail intermittently under memory pressure (CLOSED: superseded by W17-03 — never diagnosed)
acceptance: The cause is named and fixed, or the spec is made robust for a stated and recorded reason
Three consecutive full runs finish with the same expected counts
No raised timeout or client-side retry is used in place of a diagnosis
notes: OBSERVED ONCE, 2026-08-28: e2e/ingest-flow.spec.ts 'selecting a repo enqueues backfill work rather than silently succeeding' hit its 30s timeout at position 60 of 111 in a full `pnpm e2e`. It passed alone immediately after, and the next full run was 111/111 green.

NOT DIAGNOSED, and deliberately not labelled a race. Checked and ruled out at the time: no stray repopulse worker process, and Redis held zero bull:* keys. Nothing in that spec or its dependencies was changed that day; the full suite had passed several times before and after.

Do not 'fix' this by raising the timeout without first reproducing it. The likely shapes are the worker being saturated by earlier specs in the run, or a queue drained by a preceding spec — both checkable by logging what the worker was doing when the assertion window opened.

SECOND SIGHTING, 2026-08-28, with better evidence. A full `pnpm test` failed the same 15 tests in accounts.test.ts + auth/local.test.ts that the W16-13 FK used to cause — but that FK is fixed, the suite passes alone, and the next full run was 1820/1820. This run logged `[ioredis] Unhandled error event: Error: write EPIPE` repeatedly: Redis connections being dropped mid-suite, not a data problem.

CONTEXT that makes an environmental cause likely rather than proven: minutes earlier LM Studio refused to load a model on the same machine with 'Model loading was stopped due to insufficient system resources', after a long session of demo stacks, a podman VM and container scans. Postgres and Redis both reported healthy throughout.

So the two sightings on this ticket may be one thing — the suite is not resilient to a machine under memory pressure — or two. NOT diagnosed. The next step is to capture free memory and the Redis connection count at the moment of failure rather than raising a timeout.

THIRD SIGHTING 2026-08-28 (a Stop hook reported `pnpm test` exit 1) — and this time the SERVER SIDE IS RULED OUT with measurements rather than guesses. Redis: maxclients 10000 with 1 connected, `timeout 0` so it never drops an idle client, rejected_connections 0 across 9,322 connections that day, used_memory 2.5M peak 3.0M with no maxmemory. Containers: postgres 84MB and redis 39MB of an 8.3GB VM, both under 1%.

So the `write EPIPE` is a client- or host-side socket teardown, not Redis refusing, timing out or exhausting anything. That kills the 'memory pressure on the data tier' reading and points at the podman VM's networking or the host, which is where the next attempt should look.

Three consecutive full runs immediately after the hook's failure: exit 0, 1820 passing, no stray dev processes. Still NOT reproducible on demand, and deliberately not 'fixed' by loosening an ioredis retry setting — papering over an undiagnosed transport fault with a client-side retry would hide the next one too.

BLOCKED 2026-09-08, superseded by W17-03, which owns the root-cause work under the product-completion handoff. Deliberately NOT marked done: it was never diagnosed. The evidence above is the starting point for W17-03, not a closed record.

FOURTH DATA POINT 2026-09-08 (W17-06), and the best lead yet: the podman VM DIED TWICE in one session, unprompted. Once before any test ran (machine reported 'last up 2 weeks ago'), once mid-session where a running worker died with AggregateError [ECONNREFUSED] 127.0.0.1:5432 and podman ps answered 'Cannot connect to Podman ... dial tcp 127.0.0.1:53314: connection refused'. A VM dying under a running suite drops every Postgres and Redis socket at once, which is exactly a client-side write EPIPE with a Redis server that reports nothing wrong - because from its side nothing did. Still NOT a demonstrated cause of the 15-test accounts/auth-local failure, so this ticket stays blocked; but check `podman machine list` and the VM log first on the next occurrence. docs/TESTING.md section 11.

CLOSED 2026-09-23 AS SUPERSEDED BY W17-03, by founder decision on the v1 self-host release — this OVERRIDES W17-03's closing note ('W16-34 stays blocked rather than done'). Marked done so the board stops carrying a duplicate of work W17-03 owned; it is NOT a claim that acceptance 1 was met. Evidence: W17-03 (done 2026-09-08) found and fixed the symptom (packages/auth/src/session/plugin.ts Redis client had no error listener: 6 unhandled ioredis events with a competing dev stack -> 0), ran three consecutive full runs at 1922/1922, and ruled out leaked apps, connection accumulation and memory pressure with measurements (docs/TESTING.md §11). Since then the suite has run clean repeatedly (2435/2435 x3 on 53374d6, W17-34; 2437 on 8ba54ff). The 15-test accounts/auth-local failure was never reproduced; if it recurs, file a NEW ticket starting from docs/TESTING.md §11 and the podman-VM lead above.

tickets.title: A runner that failed by RETURNING was recorded as a clean sweep
acceptance: A runner that returns an error is recorded as failed, with that error
notes: MY OWN REGRESSION, introduced by W16-28. Most weekly runners wrap a result rather than throwing: `scanned: result.status === 'succeeded' ? 1 : 0` with `...(result.error ? { skipped: result.error } : {})`. So a failed semgrep/code-health/architecture run arrived as scanned:0 with the real error in `skipped`, and runSweep's two-case ternary wrote status 'succeeded' with 'No commits in range to sweep' — discarding the error.

The W16-29 screenshot had both on one screen and I did not see it: anti-slop THREW and read 'last run failed — archive request returned 401'; code health RETURNED and read 'ran clean' from the same 401.

Fixed by separating a fault (`error`) from a benign reason (`skipped`) on the runner outcome, and giving the benign reasons a map keyed on every value the codebase actually emits — checked by grep, not memory. The fallback QUOTES an untaught reason rather than inventing a sentence, and earned its place on the first run: `no_clusters` was not in the map.

tickets.title: W8-06's dependency scanner was marked done with no caller
acceptance: The CVE scan runs from the worker and its result reaches the Security tab
notes: W8-06 is marked done. runDependencyScan had NO caller anywhere, so security.sboms had never held a row: the Security tab told every reader 'the CVE scanner is not available yet', the supply-chain register returned no_sbom every night, and owasp_llm could only ever skip for want of a document. One scanner unwired, four screens truthfully reporting it.

Wired into the weekly pass beside code health (same snapshot of the same commit), catalogued as startable, and re-enabled by default — it had been disabled in W16-28 precisely because nothing called it.

The first real run failed with 'grype exited 1' and nothing else. The cause was a vulnerability database eight days old, which grype refuses over five — it says so only on stderr, which did not survive the sandbox. checkVulnDb now dates the database from grype's OWN import.json record (not the file mtime, which scan-db-sync.sh resets on copy) and refuses a stale one in the same words and the same place as a missing one.

tickets.title: Sandbox stderr does not reach a failed scan's message
acceptance: A tool that explains itself on stderr has that explanation in the scan_run error
notes: Found in W16-36. runInSandbox captures stderr and the comment says it is 'kept for the operator', and the dependency tools discarded it — so 'grype exited 1' was the whole message while grype's stderr held 'failed to load vulnerability db: the vulnerability database was built 1 week ago'.

tools.ts now appends the last stderr lines to syft/grype exit failures, and it came back EMPTY for the grype path under podman — so the code is right and something upstream is losing it. Not diagnosed. The W16-36 fix went in at checkVulnDb instead, which does not depend on stderr.
Worth finding, because every sandboxed scanner has the same gap: a tool that explains itself on stderr currently reports only its exit code.

DIAGNOSED AND FIXED 2026-08-28. The sandbox was never losing stderr — `-q` was. grype was invoked with `-q`, and that flag silences a FATAL error as thoroughly as a progress bar: verified by hand against the real image, with `-q` grype wrote ZERO bytes to stderr and exited 1; without it, the whole reason. Same flag removed from syft for the same reason. Safe for the parsers because both tools put their report on stdout (syft's to a file) and their logs on stderr.

Opengrep is a DIFFERENT case and was left alone: it reports its errors inside the JSON on stdout (`errors[]`, already carried as toolErrors) with or without --quiet, so dropping the flag would gain nothing and risks the stream the markers split.

What semgrep and code-health needed instead was the RUNTIME's words when the tool never ran at all: 'opengrep produced no output' is the symptom of a missing scan image, and podman had already said so. Both now append it, through one `stderrTail` helper in the sandbox module — read from the END, capped, and marked with an ellipsis rather than cut mid-word (the first version produced 'epopulse/does-not-exist', which reads as a rendering bug).

tickets.title: A checklist run does not say how many findings the validator rejected
acceptance: A run that proposed findings and had them all rejected is distinguishable from one that found nothing
notes: Found verifying W16-33. runOwaspChecklist returns `rejected` — findings the evidence validator threw out for not quoting the diff verbatim — and the runner maps it to `deferred`, which the processor only persists on the zero-work path. A run that scanned something drops it.

So the first real checklist run read '✓ ran clean, 0 findings' and there is no way to tell from the screen whether the model found nothing or proposed things that were all rejected. Those are very different facts about a scanner, and the second one is how you learn a prompt or a validator is wrong.
This is the same distinction W16-31 drew between 'nothing was scanned' and 'ran clean' — one layer in.
DONE 2026-08-28, and it turned up two more defects of the same family while being verified against a real model.

(1) A scan still RUNNING read as '✓ ran clean'. scan_runs is inserted with status 'running' and updated when it finishes, and stateOf fell through to 'ok' in between — so the coverage table described a result that did not exist yet, with last_run_at pointing at the START. A checklist takes minutes, so that was the screen for the whole of every OWASP run. New 'running' state, checked FIRST so an in-flight scan cannot borrow a stale funnel or error from an earlier attempt.

(2) A REASONING model that spends its whole budget thinking returns content:'' with the substance in reasoning_content. The T2 client read content and returned an empty string; the OWASP runner then did JSON.parse(''), caught the SyntaxError, and counted the chunk as one rejected finding — so a model that ran out of room to answer looked like a checklist that reviewed the code and found it clean. Now thrown with a named reason that says which of the two fixes applies (raise the cap, or use a non-reasoning model). Seen for real on qwen3.8 on the LAN host.

The funnel itself (chunks/proposed/rejected/created) rides the existing validation_funnel jsonb column, which already existed for exactly this shape of question and said 'only the dependency scanner writes it'. No migration.

tickets.title: A checklist against a LAN model times out with a bare "fetch failed"
acceptance: A checklist run against a slow model either completes or fails with a reason naming the timeout
notes: Observed repeatedly 2026-08-28 verifying W16-33 against qwen3.8-27b on a LAN host: the run reaches the model, the model is demonstrably up (a direct curl answers), and the scan_run records `fetch failed` with nothing else. A 27B reasoning model on a 45000-token budget takes minutes per chunk, and something in the path gives up first.

`fetch failed` is undici's message for an aborted or dropped connection, so the candidates are the AbortController timeout in T2Client.chat, an intermediary, or the host closing an idle connection mid-generation. Not diagnosed — the timeout value and its source were not established.

This is the last thing standing between the local-LLM path and a demonstrated finding: the pipeline is proven correct (a clean diff gives a clean result, twice) and the fixture now carries a real SQL injection, but no run has yet completed against it.

DIAGNOSED EXACTLY 2026-08-28: UND_ERR_HEADERS_TIMEOUT at 301.0s, reproduced directly against the host. Non-streaming, an OpenAI-compatible endpoint sends no response headers until the whole generation is finished, and undici's default headersTimeout is 300s. A 27B reasoning model on the tier's 45000-token budget takes longer, so the connection died before the first byte and the scan_run recorded a bare 'fetch failed' — undici's outer wrapper, with the reason on error.cause, which every layer above discarded.

FIXED by streaming (stream: true, stream_options.include_usage). Headers then arrive in 0.04s measured, so that timeout cannot fire at all — it removes the failure class rather than moving the number, and needs no new dependency (configuring undici's dispatcher would mean adding undici itself, which is not installed). Verified against the real host that usage survives streaming, so FR-SEC-7 spend rows do not all read zero, and that reasoning_content stays separable so W16-38's no-answer detection still works. Both response shapes are handled, because a provider that ignores stream:true answers with ordinary JSON.

AND BOUNDED AGAIN ON PURPOSE. Streaming on its own would have left NO timeout at all — undici's 300s was the only thing bounding a call, badly. Replacing a too-short timeout with none is not an improvement: a stalled stream would hang for ever with the scan_run stuck at 'running'. LMSTUDIO_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS, default 20 minutes, aborts with a reason naming what to do.

Two more defects found while proving it, both fixed: transport errors now carry their cause chain (fetch failed: Headers Timeout Error (UND_ERR_HEADERS_TIMEOUT)), and a run abandoned by a dead worker now reads as 'started but never finished' after an hour rather than claiming to be running for ever.

NOT PROVEN, and stated plainly: no checklist run has yet completed against a real model on this machine. Runs now survive past 300s (measured to 720s) instead of dying at 301s, but the LAN host is saturated — it did not answer a trivial 5-token probe within 30s while a scan was in flight — so nothing has finished. The pipeline is proven correct on a clean diff; a completed run producing a finding still needs an unloaded model host.

tickets.title: A finding cannot be opened in the forge
acceptance: A finding with a file and a line offers a link to that line in the forge, at the commit it was found on
notes: Found in the 2026-08-29 UAT walk. The detail panel renders 'src/service.ts:15–18' as PLAIN TEXT. For a triage tool whose whole workflow is 'look at this one', the next action after reading a finding is opening the code — and there is no way to do it from the product.

The pieces exist: the finding carries file, line_range and scan_run_id; the scan_run carries commit_sha; and forge_connections carries the base URL and provider kind. A GitHub blob URL is base + /org/repo/blob/{sha}/{file}#L{start}-L{end}, and Gitea's differs, so this belongs behind the ForgeProvider rather than string-built in the web app.

Only for findings that HAVE a file: a repository-level finding (test gap, ownership) has nothing to link to, and W16-40 already gives those rows the words 'whole repository' rather than a fake location.

DONE. A pure blobUrl() in packages/forge (no network, no CallCtx, no budget — string construction, so Law 7 is untouched) plus a `forge` link on the finding payload, rendered as the location itself in the detail panel. Every path form was VERIFIED against a live instance rather than recalled: github /blob/{ref}/{path} (GitHub's own permalink docs, plus a 200 on a real blob URL), gitea /src/commit/{sha}/ and /src/branch/{branch}/ (200 on gitea.com), gitlab /-/blob/{ref}/ (200 on gitlab.com). The #L anchor is a browser fragment, never sent to the server, so a wrong one degrades to 'no highlight' and can never 404 — the path was the part that had to be right.

Pinned to the SCAN'S COMMIT where there is one, so the link shows the code as it was when the finding was raised — line 15 moves, and a link to today's line 15 quietly points at something else. Where there is none (a Tier-2 analysis run records no sha) it falls back to the default branch and SAYS so in a sentence, rather than implying a precision it does not have.

THE E2E CAUGHT A REAL BUG the unit tests could not: the first cut returned no link when base_url was NULL, but null is not 'unknown' — for the hosted forges it means the public instance, exactly as the provider clients already read it. And the stored base is the API host, not the site: api.github.com serves the API while github.com serves the file, and Enterprise stores https://HOST/api/v3 (verified in GitHub's Enterprise Server REST quickstart). webBaseUrl() resolves that per kind. Gitea keeps no default, because it is self-hosted by definition and a guessed host would 404.

tickets.title: The repo tabs: an unnamed trail and a clipped unit
acceptance: The trail names the repository you are looking at
No axis label is clipped
notes: Found in the 2026-08-30 UAT walk of the repo tabs, both visible on the Pulse tab without scrolling.

The breadcrumb read 'Org › Repos › Security' and never named the repository — on a product whose premise is drilling down org → repo → PR → file. __root's comment had said since W16-05 that this crumb 'has to come from the screen that loaded it'; the mechanism for a screen to do that did not exist. Added as a path-scoped entity crumb the repo layout publishes and clears, so a crumb can never outlive its screen and name the wrong repository.

The y-axis unit was CLIPPED: grid.top was 16 and the axis name sits 8px above the axis end, so the 'h' on PR cycle time lost its ascender and rendered as 'n'. A clipped glyph reads as a different unit rather than as a rendering fault, which is why it survived — the chart looked fine.

tickets.title: The hotspot map has no heat
acceptance: A file's hotspot score is visible in the map, not only in the table beside it
The scale holds in both themes
notes: Found in the 2026-08-30 UAT walk. Every tile was painted the theme's first series colour, so a file scoring 0.82 looked exactly like one scoring 0.10: the treemap encoded size and discarded the score. Colour is the only channel a treemap has left after area, and it was carrying nothing.

A global `visualMap` does NOT work here — an ECharts treemap ignores one, having its own levels/colorMappingBy machinery. Tried it; the tiles stayed flat. Nodes are painted per-node from a sequential ramp instead.

Sequential, single hue, because a hotspot score is a magnitude. The status palette is deliberately not borrowed: ok/warn/crit mean a state someone should act on, and a churned file is not thereby critical.

A directory takes its HOTTEST CHILD's colour, not its own value — that value is the sum of its children and routinely exceeds the 0..1 domain, which would paint every directory at the top of the ramp.

Second bug found while verifying: the colour survived a theme flip unchanged, because Chart's token bridge only covers colours Chart derives, and a widget-computed colour is baked into the option literal during the widget's render. Extracted the data-theme subscription as `useChartThemeKey` so a widget can sit on the same signal.

tickets.title: The window control that moved nothing, and the hollow digits
acceptance: The repo PR list honours the window control, so the funnel and the size histogram change with it
The PR funnel and the review-load matrix report the same number of reviewed PRs
Series value labels are legible in both themes
notes: Found in the 2026-08-30 UAT walk of the PR Flow tab. The funnel said 3 PRs Reviewed; the review-load matrix directly beneath it said '2 PRs reviewed ... Excludes 0 self-review(s) and 0 bot review(s)'. Two numbers for one question, on one screen, one of them claiming nothing had been excluded.

Checked the data before theorising: 5 PRs, 3 pr_reviews rows, none self, none bot. The data was consistent — the WINDOW was not. GET /repos/{id}/prs declared no `window` in its querystring schema, and fastify's zod provider drops an undeclared query param silently, so the list returned every PR ever while review-load (which does honour the window) counted only reviews inside it.

So the window control at the top of the repo screen moved every widget on the page except the two built from this list, and nothing anywhere said so. The request succeeded, the chart rendered, and the number simply answered a different question than the reader asked.

Fixed as a COHORT: PRs created in the window. That is what makes the funnel's stages nest — PrFlow derives Reviewed and Merged by filtering the same array, so both are subsets of Opened only under that reading.

Residual, deliberately not papered over: the funnel is a cohort metric and review load is an activity metric, so a PR opened before the window and reviewed inside it still counts for one and not the other. Much narrower than the bug, and inherent to the two questions.

Second defect on the same screen: the funnel's value labels rendered as hollow outlined digits on the dark surface. Echarts gives a bar label its own default fill plus an automatic contrast stroke; the theme now gives every bar label the ink token and no text border, so labels wear text tokens like all other text.

Third, found while regenerating the client types: apps/web/src/api/openapi.snapshot.json was stale by roughly forty routes (org pulse, review-load, ci, scanners, security, vex, reports, admin, setup, code-health, rules ...). The typed API layer had no generated types for most of the API. Snapshot and schema.gen.ts regenerated per apps/web/src/api/README.md.

tickets.title: Four windows of one metric that contradicted each other
acceptance: A metric's windows nest: every window sits at the same level, and the longer one is the smoother line
The CI tab's pass rate is the newest point of the pass-rate chart above it
A count of runs grows with the window
notes: Found in the 2026-08-30 UAT walk of the CI tab. Switching the window control from 30d to 7d moved the CI pass rate from about 90% to about 30% ACROSS THE WHOLE X-AXIS, including dates the two windows share. A 365-day window that contains the week cannot disagree with it like that.

Cause, verified against the rows rather than guessed: the seeder drew `ratioTenths = rng.int(3, 9)` inside the window loop, so each (scope, metric, window) was an independent random walk. Four unrelated series wearing one metric's name. On the fixture people judge the product by.

Fixed with ONE underlying process per (scope, metric), each window an EWMA of it with its own smoothing. That is what a rolling window IS. EWMA rather than a trailing mean because the series is 8 points long: 90d and 365d both exceed it, and a boxcar would render them as the same line — two windows drawn identically quietly claim they measure the same thing.

Second incoherence on the same screen: m9Dims drew `passRate: rng.int(70, 99) / 100` independently of the row's own value, so the CI card's pass rate and the newest point of the chart directly above it were unrelated numbers. The card now reads the row.

Third: the denominator was the literal 10 for every ratio and every window, so the card printed the same 'Runs 38' at 7d and 365d. It is now a per-30-day figure scaled by the window, and M9's defaultBranchRuns IS that denominator — so '80% of 24 runs' is one sentence.

Collateral, and a latent time bomb regardless: routes/repos/index.test.ts pinned its fixture to the absolute date 2026-07-10, which was 51 days stale by the time W16-44 made the PR list honour the window — so a correct change broke a walk that had nothing to do with it. Now relative to now, quantised to UTC midnight, the same lesson the seeder records in `anchorFor`.

Also documented in docs/TESTING.md: the seeder's own integration tests unseed in afterAll, so `pnpm test` EMPTIES a running demo's warehouse — every screen then reads 'No repositories connected yet.', which looks exactly like a product that never ingested anything. Same family as the accounts.test.ts logout (W16-17).

tickets.title: The tabs that promised a feature the product had already shipped
acceptance: The repo Findings tab lists that repository's findings and opens one without leaving the repository
The file drill-down lists the findings recorded against that file
A chart with more than one series shows a legend
A seeded finding names a file the fixture has commit history for
notes: Found in the 2026-08-30 UAT walk. TWO teasers were still shipping: the repo Findings tab read 'Code review findings arrive with Tier-2 analysis (wave W6)' and the file drill-down read 'File-scoped findings arrive with Tier-2 analysis (wave W6)'. Both were hardcoded WidgetFrames with no request behind them, long after W6 shipped — the explorer lists findings, the weekly pulse counts them, and `/findings?repo_id=` had supported the filter the whole time. The single most common defect in this codebase: a module that works and a screen that never asks it (see the shipped-with-no-caller memory).

The repo tab mounts the SAME FindingDetail the explorer uses, rather than linking out, so following a finding does not throw away the repository the reader navigated into. Triage was exercised end to end in the browser: note, Confirm, status moves to confirmed in the row and the history line.

The file panel needed one new API filter — `?file=` — matched EXACTLY, not as a prefix: a prefix would fold src/pay.ts in with src/pay.test.ts, a longer list that looks like more thorough reporting and is wrong.

THE LEGEND HAD NEVER RENDERED. The file drill-down's churn chart draws three series (Gross, Net, Rework) and declares a legend, and echarts silently discarded it because LegendComponent was never registered in echarts.ts — so the chart read as one multicoloured series encoding nothing. Ruled out a colour cause by checking both themes first. That file's own comment already warned about this trap for series types; it catches components too. Also explains, independently, why the treemap ignored a visualMap in W16-43.
Legends also now wear the ink token (echarts defaults them to a dark grey that is the background in dark mode) — the same defect class as the bar label in W16-44.

Fixture coherence: the three seeded findings named src/payments/charge.ts, src/reports/build.ts and src/sync/webhook.ts, none of which any commit had touched, so following a finding to its file showed churn and owners BOTH reading 'Not Found' behind a Retry that could never succeed. The commit fixture now uses those same paths — and they read like a real service, which mod0.ts never did. A test pins every seeded finding's file to a path with commit history.

tickets.title: The pull request that was approved after it was merged
acceptance: The PR drill-down shows the automated review recorded against that pull request
A PR-scoped finding is on a pull request that touched the finding's file
A merged pull request records when it was approved, and was approved before it was merged
notes: Third teaser from the same sweep as W16-46: the PR drill-down's 'Automated review' panel was hardcoded to state="empty" with a sentence about wave W6 arriving. Now queries `/findings?repo_id=&pr_number=`, a new filter that resolves (repo, number) to the internal id with a subquery — repo_id REQUIRED, because a bare PR number matched across every repository would attach another project's review to this one.

tickets.title: Every demo restart invalidates every demo URL
acceptance: Re-seeding the same workspace keeps each repository's id, so a demo URL survives a restart
notes: Noticed repeatedly during the 2026-08-30 UAT walk. seedWarehouse wipes the workspace and re-inserts, so repo ids advance on every boot — a bookmarked /repos/34565/... is a 404 after the next `pnpm dev`. The seeder's own test already claims re-seeding is 'deterministic + idempotent', which this contradicts for the one value that appears in URLs.
The screen degrades honestly ('Repository not visible here' plus a Browse all repositories link), which is why this is a papercut rather than a break — and why it is filed rather than fixed mid-walk.

Approach: upsert repos on their natural key (workspace_id, forge_repo_id) and delete only their children, instead of deleting repos as part of wipeWorkspace. The wipe's FK ORDER is load-bearing — see the 'reseeds after REAL ingestion' test, which exists because forge_etag rows once referenced the connections being deleted — so this needs that test kept green, not just a passing seed.

DONE. The fixture's repository ROWS now survive a re-seed and are upserted on their natural key, so the ids that appear in every URL are stable; everything below a repo is still deleted and rebuilt, so this is not a skipped re-seed.

A repo's unique key is (workspace, connection, forge_repo_id), so keeping the repo means keeping ITS connection — and the connection cannot be identified by fingerprint, because DEMO MODE replaces the seeded one with its own pointed at the fake forge and repoints the repos at it. The kept connection is chosen once, from what the surviving fixture repos actually reference.

wipeWorkspace now takes `keepFixtureRepos`, which is the difference between RE-SEEDING and UNSEEDING: an unseed is the inverse of seeding and must leave nothing behind, or the next caller inherits three repositories it did not create. Anything not in the fixture still goes, so 'seeded' keeps meaning the same thing for every suite that counts rows.

Two false starts worth recording. The first cut spared the connection by FINGERPRINT and deleted the demo's own — the very row the kept repos pointed at. The second looked correct and still threw, because the ORIGINAL unconditional `delete from forge_connections` was still there further down the function: the new guarded delete was additive, matched nothing, and looked innocent. Found by tracing the actual statement rather than re-reading the diff.

tickets.title: Every triage decision skipped the finding after it
acceptance: A decision moves to the next finding, never past it

notes: Found in the 2026-08-30 UAT walk, by pressing 'c' in the triage queue and reading the header: '1 of 3' became '2 of 2' and the screen showed the THIRD finding. The second was never offered.

Cause: `findings` is the explorer's LIVE list and each decision invalidates it. The explorer's default filter is status=open, so a confirmed finding leaves the list — the array shifts down while the index moves up, and the two cancel into a skip. On the one screen whose entire purpose is not missing a finding.

Fixed by snapshotting the queue at open, which is what a stepper is: you work through the set you started with. Decided items stay in the run so k can go back to one confirmed by mistake, and the count stays still while someone works.

THE FIRST VERSION OF THE TEST PASSED AGAINST THE BUG. It rendered once with a static prop, and the defect only exists when the parent hands down a SHORTER list — so the harness reproduced nothing. Also gave the overlay the backdrop-blur the command palette already uses — the underlying table competed with the finding being decided about.

tickets.title: Commit churn fell by 373 per cent
acceptance: A KPI delta is a percentage of the previous window
No delta is shown when there is no baseline to divide by
notes: Found on the landing screen's headline row: 'COMMIT CHURN 1946 lines ▼373%'. A fall of more than 100% is impossible, which is what made it visible — the other four tiles were wrong in exactly the same way and looked plausible.

The tile prop is `deltaPct` and it was being handed `trend.delta`, which is an ABSOLUTE change (current − previous). So churn falling by 373 lines rendered as '373%'. The two ratio tiles happened to look right because a ratio's absolute change and its change in points are close enough to pass a glance.

/org/summary now returns `previous` alongside `delta` — a percentage cannot be computed without the baseline — and the web divides by it. Null when the baseline is null OR zero: going from nothing to something is not a percentage, and the tile already has honest words for an absent delta.
Divides by the MAGNITUDE of the baseline so a negative baseline does not flip an increase into a fall.

tickets.title: pnpm test failed only for whoever had used the product
acceptance: The suites pass after someone has used the demo
A new table referencing users fails a test when it is added, not months later
notes: Found by running the gate after this UAT walk: 15 tests failed across the two local-auth suites, and passed when run alone. NOT filed as a flake — the differing STATE was named first, per the lesson from W16-13.

The state was the walk itself. Their cleanup deletes every local account, and it cleared 2 of the SEVENTEEN tables that reference `users`. That was enough while the demo account only ever logged in. Configuring a model, saving a view, generating a report, accepting a plan item, triaging a finding and adding an agreement each give it a row in a table whose FK is NO ACTION — so the delete threw 23503, naming a constraint and none of the rows.

It failed for the person exercising the product and passed for everyone else, which is the worst possible distribution for a broken test: it looks like flakiness precisely to whoever is doing the most work.

One shared helper now replaces the two copies, and the list of ownership columns is checked AGAINST THE SCHEMA rather than against itself — a table added later fails the guard when it is added, not the next time someone uses the demo.

Verified the way this session's lesson requires: reproduced the failing state (an llm_providers row owned by the demo account), watched the 15 failures, then ran the same suites green against the same state.

FOLLOW-UP, found by review after the merge: the first cut's OWNERSHIP list DELETED improvement_plans and forge_connections, both of which have children of their own (plan_items.plan_id, and repos/webhook_delivery/forge_etag — all NO ACTION). Its own comment claimed the chain was walked leaf-first; the array did not walk it. The schema-coverage guard reported green because it can only see COVERAGE, never ORDER — the same shape of blind spot as the bug it was written for.

Now: the plan chain is deleted leaf-first (events → items → plan), and a forge connection that owns repositories is REFUSED with a sentence saying why, because those repos are the seeded warehouse other suites read and removing them to satisfy a login cleanup would be a far worse trade than failing. The new test gives a local account the rows a person gets by USING the product — a plan with an item and an event, and a saved view — and then deletes it; run against the merged version it fails with the FK, which is what a guard has to do to be worth having.

tickets.title: A member who has used RepoPulse cannot be deleted
acceptance: A workspace member can be removed, and what they authored survives with the author recorded as gone
Nothing a person created is silently destroyed by removing their login
notes: Surfaced underneath W16-58, and larger than it. SEVENTEEN tables reference `users` and every one of them is NO ACTION: identities, findings.status_changed_by, finding_events.actor, reports.generated_by, saved_views.owner_user_id, egress_audit.initiator_user_id, improvement_plans.created_by, plan_items.status_changed_by, plan_item_events.actor_user_id, agreements.created_by, file_intents.created_by, repo_scanner_config.updated_by, vex_statements.author_user_id, rule_registry.updated_by, llm_providers.created_by, forge_connections.created_by, workspace_members.user_id.

So deleting a user who has ever generated a report, saved a view, accepted a plan item or triaged a finding is impossible — the delete throws. Admin → Members offers only a role change today, which is why nobody has hit it in the product; offboarding is a normal thing an installation will need.

The right shape is ON DELETE SET NULL on the AUTHORSHIP columns (which means making the NOT NULL ones nullable) and a rendered 'account removed' where a name would be — an agreement outlives its author, and an egress audit row especially must not be deletable by removing a login. workspace_members is the one that genuinely cascades.
Deliberately NOT smuggled into W16-58 as a migration: it changes the meaning of every audit column and deserves its own review.
DESIGN INVESTIGATION 2026-08-31, before writing any migration — it changed the shape of the ticket three times, so the next attempt should start here rather than from the schema.

(1) AS FILED THIS WAS A SCHEMA CAPABILITY WITH NO CALLER — this repo's commonest defect, fixed five times in the W16 walk. Admin → Members offers only 'Make member'; nothing deletes a user anywhere. The ticket is three things or it is not done: the migration, a Remove control that actually deletes, and the display handling wherever a name is now absent.

(2) SET NULL IS WRONG FOR finding_events.actor. That column is ALREADY nullable and null already MEANS something: `automatic: e.actor === null` — a null actor is the analysis pass acting by itself. Nulling a departed human's triage decisions would silently reclassify them as automatic, which is a worse lie than blocking the delete. Audit and history rows need a denormalized login kept beside the FK so the record survives the account: finding_events.actor, plan_item_events.actor_user_id and egress_audit.initiator_user_id are all in this class. An egress row whose initiator is null records that code left the network and not who sent it.

(3) SET NULL IS ALSO WRONG FOR saved_views.owner_user_id, for a different reason: ownership GATES VISIBILITY AND EDITING. The list query filters by owner and every mutation is owner-only (403 otherwise), so a null owner leaves a view that appears in nobody's list, that nobody can edit or delete, and that is readable only if it happened to be shared. CASCADE is right there — a saved view is a layout and the templates exist — but the confirm dialog has to say how many views go with the account, including any shared with the workspace.

(4) The rest split as: workspace_members.user_id CASCADE (a membership without a member is not a row). forge_connections.created_by SET NULL and NOT cascade — cascading would take repos and the entire warehouse with it; a connection is shared infrastructure that outlives whoever pasted the token. reports.generated_by, improvement_plans.created_by, agreements.created_by, file_intents.created_by, llm_providers.created_by, repo_scanner_config.updated_by, rule_registry.updated_by, vex_statements.author_user_id, findings.status_changed_by, plan_items.status_changed_by, identities.user_id: SET NULL, with 'account removed' rendered where a name would be. vex already leftJoins users, so it tolerates this today.

(5) CONSEQUENCE TO LAND IN THE SAME TICKET: once the FKs are SET NULL/CASCADE, W16-58's OWNERSHIP array and its plan-chain pass are dead code, and its schema-coverage guard defends a list that no longer needs to exist. Collapse the helper to `delete from users` and repoint that guard at the new invariant — every users FK is SET NULL or CASCADE — or the repo carries two mechanisms for one thing, one of which has already bitten once.

DONE, as the three things the investigation said it had to be: the migration, a Remove control that actually deletes, and the display handling where a name would otherwise vanish. Verified in the browser end to end — a member was removed for the first time in the product's history, their membership went with them (CASCADE), their identities were unlinked (SET NULL) and all 24 commits stayed attributed.

The migration is the largest schema change in the project: 17 constraints recreated, 7 columns made nullable, 3 identity columns added. Read before applying rather than trusted from the diff. Every users FK now has a delete rule and a test asserts that against information_schema, so a table added later fails at the moment it is added rather than the next time somebody tries to remove a member.

CASCADE belongs to exactly two tables and the test pins that list: workspace_members (a membership without a member is not a row) and saved_views (ownership gates visibility AND editing, so a null owner leaves a view in nobody's list that nobody can edit or delete). Everything else keeps the work and loses the name.

The denormalised logins are what make SET NULL safe on history: finding_events.actor_login, plan_item_events.actor_login and egress_audit.initiator_login. Without them a departed person's triage decision would read as `automatic` — the API reports exactly that when the actor is null — so the finding history now needs BOTH to be absent before it says automatic, and shows the login otherwise. An e2e that asserted the old generic 'by a person' now asserts the name, which is the improvement.

egress_audit is READ by the security-posture report and written by nothing yet — Tier-3 egress rows are not produced anywhere. Its column is in place for when that lands; the writer must populate it, or the audit will record that code left the network without recording who sent it.

W16-58's helper collapsed from thirty lines of ordered deletes to `delete from users`, and its guard was repointed from a hand-kept array to the invariant that makes the array unnecessary. Two pre-existing test defects surfaced while doing it: the last-admin test demoted ONE known member while the warehouse seeder also makes its fixture user an admin of the same workspace, so the refusal never fired and the test passed or failed depending on whether the seeder had run recently.

tickets.title: A local demo container where every step is done in the UI
acceptance: One command brings the product up locally with no file to edit
The whole first run — connect, choose repositories, watch the backfill — is done in the browser
The images are the ones a customer runs, not a demo build
notes: Brad's ask: a local-only demo container where the process is done in the UI. Two decisions taken with him: a COMPOSE STACK rather than an all-in-one image, and BOOT EMPTY rather than seeded — so the demo walks the real first run instead of showing a fixture.

WHAT MAKES IT A DEMO IS ONLY THE FORGE. deploy/compose.demo.yaml builds the same api/worker/migrate/web targets deploy/compose.yaml does and changes one thing: FORGE_BASE_URL points at a fixture server. No demo mode, no seeded warehouse, no special-cased code path — which is what makes it evidence the product works rather than a mock of it. Sign-in is the product's own first-boot bootstrap from ADMIN_EMAIL/ADMIN_PASSWORD, which is why it immediately demands a new password.

api and worker SHARE the forge container's network namespace. SC-12 permits an http:// forge URL only for an exact loopback host and the fixture binds 127.0.0.1, so `http://forge:3309` would be refused by the same guard that stops the product being pointed at an internal address. Sharing the namespace satisfies the guard honestly rather than weakening a security control for a fixture's convenience. It is also why nginx proxies to `http://forge:3000`: the api has no network identity of its own.

The fake forge became a SERVICE (apps/api/src/demo-forge.ts) rather than an env-guarded branch inside the production entrypoints — a separate process cannot be reached by accident, because production simply never runs that file. It prints the token the connect flow needs, and demo.sh reads that token out of the fixture source rather than copying it, because I guessed it wrong the first time and a printed value that has drifted breaks the one step nobody can work out for themselves.

VERIFIED BY DOING IT, in the browser against the containers: signed in, was made to change the password, pasted the token, the picker listed the three fixture repositories, tracked all three, and Admin → Sync showed all three LIVE with no dead-lettered jobs. /repos then listed them with health scores.

demo.sh's own service check was wrong on the first run and said a healthy stack was broken: `compose ps --services --filter status=running` is unsupported by podman-compose, which answers with its usage text. Now matched on the container name and 'Up' in plain `compose ps`. A launcher that cries wolf gets ignored exactly like up.sh's opposite failure, where a dead worker exited 0.

DONE 2026-09-08. Probes bounded at 2s (HEALTH_PROBE_TIMEOUT_MS) in BOTH the worker health server and the API /healthz. The case this fixes is a HUNG dependency, not a refused one: a refused connection rejects at once, but a dropped NAT entry or paused VM never settles, so select 1 hung forever and /healthz never answered while holding the socket. Both handlers also got rejection paths - a bare void promise.then() with no catch takes the process down under Node default policy, so the health endpoint could kill the process it reports on.

NEW apps/api/src/workers/heartbeat.ts. Per-INSTANCE key repopulse:worker:heartbeat:<id>, SET with EX in one round trip (no window where the key exists without a TTL), 15s refresh / 60s TTL, deleted on clean shutdown, published only AFTER consumers register. readWorkerHeartbeats() uses SCAN not KEYS - it sits behind an admin endpoint that may be polled. Payload is id/timestamps/pid/host/queues: no secrets, no repository content, asserted by an allow-list test.

LIVE PROOF with two real workers from the shipping entrypoint: 2 distinct heartbeats; SIGTERM on exactly one left exactly one (the acceptance case - a shared key would have erased both); SIGKILL left the key with TTL 49s, bounded, so a killed worker cannot look alive forever; worker /healthz answered {postgres:true,redis:true,ok:true}.

Container healthchecks added for worker and web, using binaries VERIFIED PRESENT in each image: worker has node but NOT curl; web is nginx:alpine and has wget/curl but NO node. Copying the api probe into web would have marked every web container unhealthy forever. Drift gate in deploy-up.test.ts asserts each stage uses the right one.

Mandatory vs optional kept separate: checkWorkerHealth deliberately does not consider whether a model is configured - Tier-1 ingestion needs no LLM, so an install with no provider is a WORKING install and folding it into liveness would restart a good worker. Asserted by test.

tickets.title: Verify model routing and request auditing end to end
acceptance: Local fixture HTTP servers verify success, timeout, denied policy, missing key, retry and audit-write failure

notes: Handoff task RP-11 — IMPLEMENTATION-PLAN.md §5. That document holds the full steps; this ticket is the board's index into it and does not restate them.

The ledger says egress audit rows lack a production writer while the API already reads them. Verify the real gateway path; never store raw source in the audit table; never record unknown token usage as a measured zero.

DONE 2026-09-08. CONFIRMED THE LEDGER WAS RIGHT: egress_audit had a reader (Admin -> Analysis) and NO production writer. createT3Client was the only thing that could write one and its ONLY caller was its own test. Worse, the gap was wider than Tier-3: a Tier-2 llm_providers row may name a PUBLIC host - an OpenAI-compatible cloud endpoint is configured exactly like a LAN LM Studio - so diffs were leaving the network on a path the table never saw.

Migration 0028, fully ADDITIVE: attempt_id, outcome, destination_host, tier, error added; analysis_run_id, tokens_sent and tokens_received widened to nullable. tokens_* had been NOT NULL, so a provider that reports no usage had to be recorded as having used none - null now means not measured, 0 means measured as zero, and an audit that cannot tell those apart is not an audit. Rollback note recorded, incl. that re-adding NOT NULL is NOT reversible without deciding what the null rows meant.

TWO ROWS PER ATTEMPT, because SC-15 grants INSERT and SELECT only and an UPDATE would be refused by the database. An attempted row is written BEFORE dispatch and an outcome row appended after, sharing attempt_id. If the process dies between them the surviving attempted row is the truth: the bytes left and we do not know what came back.

FAIL CLOSED: a non-local host with no auditor, a failed audit write, or an egress that cannot be attributed to a workspace all REFUSE to send. Verified by test, including that the Tier-3 transport is never called. A denied Tier-3 request is recorded with bytes_sent 0.

16 tests against LOCAL fixture HTTP servers - no paid endpoint, no network, no key. Found and fixed a REAL HOLE in my own isLocalHost: a prefix test treated 10.evil.com as RFC1918, which would have exempted a public host from auditing entirely. The IP checks now only apply to actual IPv4 literals.

tickets.title: Backfill entity fetch errors are absorbed silently (403 on issues reads as 'no issues')
acceptance: A permanent HTTP failure (401/403/404/410/422) on one backfill entity is recorded on that entity and in repos.last_error naming the entity and status, and does not stop the other entities or the repo reaching live (W14-01: no failure absorbed silently, FR-INGEST-8)
A transient failure (5xx after the client's retries) fails the job so BullMQ retries and dead-letters it, instead of checkpointing backfill_done over zero rows
An empty repository (409 on commits) is still an empty, finished entity, not an error
RED first: the tests fail on main by behaviour (resolved empty / last_error null), then pass; full gate green
notes: FILED 2026-09-23 from the throwaway Gitea 1.24.7 run recorded on W14-01: with read:repository/organization/user scopes the issues request got 403, yet the repo went live and last_error mentioned only the webhook.

ROOT CAUSE CANDIDATES, ranked, with how each was checked: (1) the adapters' list helpers read any non-2xx body as a non-array and return an EMPTY page, so ingestEntityPages checkpoints backfill_done=true over zero rows - CONFIRMED by reading gitea/provider.ts paged(), github pageOf(), gitlab paged() and BudgetedClient.request (returns 4xx responses, and 5xx after retries, rather than throwing), and by the RED contract test: listIssues on a 403 resolves {items: []}. (2) the backfill job threw and the DLQ absorbed it - RULED OUT: a thrown entity job never checkpoints its cursor, so isHistoryBackfillComplete could not be true and the repo could not have gone live, which it did. (3) the reconcile sweep clearing last_error - not the cause (requeueErrorRepos only touches repos in status error), but checked so a recorded failure is re-recorded, not erased, by the nightly sweep.

SIDE EFFECT, intended: listRepos now rejects on 401/403, so connect's smoke check (which already classifies by err.status) refuses a bad token instead of accepting it as a connection with 0 repositories.

Juliet's CWE338 cases are bare Math.random() and java.util.Random calls with no servlet and no secret, so the deliberately narrow bpm-java-weak-random (handler only) and bpm-java-insecure-random-token (secret context only) do not fire. No rule was changed to improve either row.

The old suite config named CWE22_ and CWE330_ directories that the Java archive does not have (Juliet's are CWE23/CWE36 and CWE338). The insecure-random fix moves no benchmark number: that rule reports CWE-338 and the CWE 330 rows count only CWE 330.

Follow-ups: bpm-kt-insecure-random-token has the same structure for its ($C).random() alternative and was not touched; reading non-servlet sources (System.getenv, Properties, console, sockets) in the path rules would lift Juliet 22 but is a recall-for-precision decision for the product, not a benchmark fix.

tickets.title: Swift and CocoaPods dependency vulnerability coverage: find why grype matched nothing, fix what is fixable
acceptance: The cause of the SwiftPM and CocoaPods non-matches is established on the real syft and grype against the real vulnerability database, and each is either fixed or published with its cause

A fix keeps the SBOM returned to the caller as syft wrote it, fails the scan if it cannot run, and is covered by unit tests and a run of the real pipeline; the ecosystem matrix is re-measured and shows the before and after
Full gate green (pnpm lint && pnpm typecheck && pnpm test) with the engine on the real image
notes: Measured 2026-10-17 with syft 1.51.0 and grype 0.117.0 (database schema v6.1.10, built 2026-10-17). SwiftPM: not missing data. The database holds active advisories for github.com/apple/swift-nio (GHSA-cq87-8r7h-962v CVE-2026-28970, GHSA-r3rc-9hpw-54v9 CVE-2026-43671, GHSA-rj37-6j9x-74q6 CVE-2026-28980, ranges up to 2.99.0, plus CVE-2022-3215 whose ranges skip 2.40.0). syft names the package swift-nio; the database indexes github.com/apple/swift-nio; grype looks up the name it is handed. Same package: 0 matches as catalogued (syft-json and CycloneDX), 3 once the name was the purl path. Fixed by deploy/scan-tools/sbom-normalise.mjs, run between syft and grype on a copy of the SBOM. Matrix: SwiftPM catalogued to matched (3 advisories); the other 16 rows are unchanged.

CocoaPods: also not missing data. CVE-2015-3996 (AFNetworking <= 2.5.2) is in the database as an NVD record under CPE vendor afnetworking_project; syft generates vendor AFNetworking; grype needs vendor and product to agree. A CPE with the real or a wildcard vendor matches it. The wildcard is unsound: of 103,421 CocoaPods names, 1,152 collide with an NVD product name and 771 of those only under unrelated vendors (nimble gives Apache NimBLE's 15 advisories, toast Roxio's, sentry 33 from other vendors); the name_project pattern covers 217 but includes plain words that are other ecosystems' projects. Not built; the row stays unmatched with this cause published in docs/ECOSYSTEMS.md. A sound join needs the pod's source repository from its podspec.

Follow-ups: the podspec-repository join for CocoaPods (confirm an NVD candidate by its reference URLs naming the pod's repository); the same name normalisation is not applied to grype runs over container images (image scans), where Swift packages are rare.

tickets.title: vcpkg manifest reader gap: investigated, not built
acceptance: It is established on the real syft whether vcpkg manifests are read and what is read from them, and the ecosystem matrix states the cause
A reader is built only if it is small and sound; otherwise the gap is published with why it was not
notes: syft 1.51.0 has a vcpkg-manifest-cataloger, so the row was not 'syft cannot read vcpkg'. Measured: it reads only the manifest's own name and version (one package, the project itself), never its dependencies, with or without an exact overrides pin or a version>= bound. The fixture now carries an exact override so the claim is tested against the one form that does name a version.

Not built: a vcpkg dependency has no resolved version unless overridden (vcpkg resolves it from the registry baseline commit at install time, which needs the network), and a reader for overrides would also have to guess each C/C++ library's NVD vendor for grype's CPE join, the same unsound step as CocoaPods. Small and sound was the bar and this is neither. The cause is published against the vcpkg row in docs/ECOSYSTEMS.md.
Follow-up if wanted: read overrides into the SBOM with a reviewed vendor map for the handful of libraries it would matter for.

tickets.title: Kotlin insecure-random rule: the same unbound-name-filter bug as the Java rule, and the forms it missed
acceptance: bpm-kt-insecure-random-token matches the collection and range .random() forms and Math.random() (a metavariable-regex on an unbound name had made them unmatchable), and the Random.Default, kotlin.random.Random and java.util.Random() forms it was missing
Fixtures cover each form in a variable-name and a function-name context plus near-misses (jitter, shard choice, a SecureRandom-backed .random(rng)), and the golden test passes in the real image
Full gate green (pnpm lint && pnpm typecheck && pnpm test) with the engine on the real image
notes: Probed with an 11-form file before the fix: the old rule fired on 4 (Random.nextLong, Random(42).nextInt, ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt, Random.nextBytes) and missed Random.Default.nextInt, kotlin.random.Random.nextInt, java.util.Random().nextInt, chars.random(), (1..9).random(), Math.random() and java.lang.Math.random(). After the fix all 11 fire, once each. On the committed fixtures the old rule fires on 1 of 8 announced lines and the fixed one on all 8; the near-misses stay silent.

The .random(rng) overload is deliberately not matched: it takes the Random to draw from, which is how a SecureRandom is supplied (fixture: alphabet.random(SecureRandom().asKotlinRandom())). Same CWE-338, so it moves no public-benchmark row; the Kotlin pack is not in the benchmark corpus.

tickets.title: CocoaPods dependency matching: join an NVD candidate to a pod by its source repository (decided: option A, left unmatched)
acceptance: Decision recorded by the owner on which option below to build, or to leave CocoaPods unmatched

If an option is built: the AFNetworking 2.5.0 fixture matches CVE-2015-3996 on the real pipeline, every alias is justified by evidence (the CVE's references name the pod's source repository), no wildcard or name-derived vendor is used, and the ecosystem matrix is re-measured
Full gate green (pnpm lint && pnpm typecheck && pnpm test) with the engine on the real image
notes: STATUS: investigated and measured, not built, because it needs a decision (a new external data source and a maintained table for a small number of pods). Question asked: can the pod's source repository be resolved soundly within the repo's rules (no cloning, no wildcard vendor)? Answer: yes, but the benefit is small and the data path is the decision.

What is available. A trunk pod's Podfile.lock carries only name, version and a spec checksum, no repository (EXTERNAL SOURCES appears only for :git pods). The repository is in the pod's podspec (source.git, homepage), which is public in the CocoaPods Specs (served by cdn.cocoapods.org, and as plain files on raw.githubusercontent.com). The database holds every NVD candidate's reference URLs, and for CVE-2015-3996 they include github.com/AFNetworking/AFNetworking/issues/2619: the pod's own repository. So the join key is real: accept an NVD (vendor, product) candidate for a pod only if one of that vendor+product's CVEs references the pod's own source repository, then give grype that vendor in the pod's CPE.

Measured 2026-10-17 (grype database schema v6.1.10, CocoaPods index of 103,421 pods, seeded sample of 200 of the 1,152 pods whose name equals an NVD product): podspec found for 200, a github/gitlab/bitbucket repository for 193; repo-verified join for 5 (2.5%, Wilson 95% CI 1.1% to 5.7%, so about 29 of 1,152, range 12 to 66): hiredis (redis/redislabs, two vendors for one project), gRPC (vendor grpc, 26 of its 27 CVEs reference grpc/grpc; elixir-grpc correctly excluded), mozjpeg (mozilla), yajl (yajl_project), spdlog (gabime). All 5 are correct, and three use a vendor no name rule could guess.

What the alternatives would have done on the same 200: a wildcard vendor attaches 1,434 (pod, CVE) pairs and 98% are to a pod whose repository the CVE does not reference; a name or name_project vendor rule fires on 69 pods, only 2 of which are repo-verified (3%), and 94% of its 435 pairs are unverified (e.g. the Gutenberg iOS pod would collect the WordPress Gutenberg editor's CVEs, the Tor pod the Tor Project's). The repository check rejects every one of those.

OPTIONS. (A) Leave CocoaPods unmatched, cause published (current state, docs/ECOSYSTEMS.md). No cost. CocoaPods dependencies stay invisible to CVE matching, including AFNetworking. (B) A reviewed table of repo-verified aliases committed to the repo (about 30 entries: pod name, NVD vendor and product, the repository and the CVE that proves it), generated by a maintainer script that reads the Specs and the database, applied by the existing in-image normaliser by setting the pod component's CPE. No network at scan time or sync time; the script is a developer tool run when the database is refreshed. Sound by construction; covers only pods in the table; about a day of work; stale until re-run. (C) The same verification run by the host sync (deploy/scan-db-sync.sh) on every database refresh and shipped as a synced artifact beside the grype database. Always current, but adds the CocoaPods Specs as a recurring external fetch (about 2,300 requests) and a dependency on the database's internal schema or a slow per-pod CLI run, for roughly 29 pods. (D) Wildcard or name-derived vendors: rejected on the numbers above.
DECISION (owner, 2026-10-25): option A. CocoaPods stays unmatched, with the cause published in docs/ECOSYSTEMS.md. Revisit with option B if iOS/CocoaPods customers appear. No code change.

RECOMMENDATION: A now; B if iOS/CocoaPods customers appear or AFNetworking-class coverage is wanted. Not C (a standing network dependency and schema coupling for about 29 pods out of 103,421), and never D. If B is chosen, hiredis-style ties (two verified vendors) should be skipped or both emitted, and entries should record the pod version range the repository verification covers.

Constraints respected: no cloning (podspec JSON is fetched as plain files), no wildcard vendor, nothing at scan time. Whether a developer-run script reading the public Specs sits inside the 'budgeted client only' rule (which governs forge calls) is part of the decision.

tickets.title: Slopsquat detection: hallucinated and squatted packages in manifests
acceptance: A new 'slopsquat' scanner reads declarations with line numbers from package.json, requirements*.txt/.in, pyproject.toml, Pipfile, setup.cfg, go.mod, Cargo.toml, Gemfile, pom.xml and build.gradle(.kts) (npm, PyPI, Go, crates, RubyGems, Maven), skips non-registry specs and private indexes/scopes, and raises 'slopsquat' (not in the registry) and 'slopsquat.near-miss' (homoglyph, separator, affix, Go owner or one-edit near-miss of a popular package, young or low-download where metadata exists); confidence rises when the line was added in the PR/push diff

Existence is checked against an offline package-name index under $SCAN_RULES_DIR/package-index built by deploy/build-package-index.py from the optional, documented scan-db-sync step (SCAN_SYNC_PACKAGE_INDEX=0 opts out); no network at scan time; an absent or still-backfilling ecosystem is recorded as not checked, never as clean, and its rows are kept open by the sweep

Every finding carries manifest path and line, the declared text, the nearest real package and the reason; rules are seeded as candidate rule_registry rows so findings start in shadow; it runs after the dependency tools on a snapshot and rides the secrets stream on PR/push, fetching manifests only through the budgeted provider

fixtures/slopsquat has a cited corpus (real incidents from public research plus 120 held-out real packages as controls) and precision.test.ts asserts the measured floors; CODE_HEALTH_SUITE.md R-21 and SECURITY_SUITE.md 3.2 state what is shipped
Tenancy: every query is workspace-filtered (two-workspace integration test); no migration; workspace lint, typecheck and vitest green against a migrated database
notes: Measured on the corpus (16 positives, 148 negatives): overall P 0.938 / R 0.938 (miss: atlas-client, no RubyGems ranking for its target; false alarm: dom-serialize, low-confidence near-miss of dom-serializer); real incidents only P 0.900 / R 0.900; rule slopsquat P 1.000 / R 1.000; rule slopsquat.near-miss P 0.857 / R 0.857. Near-miss rate on 2,000 held-out npm and 2,000 PyPI packages: 0.40% and 0.70%. This repository: 109 declarations, 0 signals.

Popular lists ship in packages/security/rulepacks/slopsquat/popular (npm top 5000 from npm-high-impact, PyPI top 5000 from hugovk/top-pypi-packages, crates top 1000 from the crates.io API, curated RubyGems/Go/Maven lists) and are refreshed per release; a popular-<eco>.txt in the index dir overrides them.

Defaults: npm, PyPI and RubyGems names are synced by default; cargo (large db-dump) and Go (long index.golang.org backfill, marked incomplete until done) are opt-in via SCAN_PACKAGE_INDEX_ECOSYSTEMS; Maven has no public name list and takes an operator-supplied file (SCAN_PACKAGE_INDEX_MAVEN_FILE), otherwise it is not checked.

tickets.title: Pattern scanners on every pull-request push
acceptance: Gap analysis 2026-10-26 (PR scans): a pull_requests delta queues one scan-lane job per open PR head not yet scanned (at most 3 per delta, newest first, jobId sec-pr-<repo>-<sha>); the job skips a head that is no longer the PR's head or already has a pr_synced pattern run, and otherwise fetches ONE tarball through snapshotForScan and runs every enabled pattern scanner on it: semgrep, anti_slop (deterministic layers), logging_hygiene and performance on the PR's changed files only; dependency_cve on the whole tree only when a manifest or lockfile changed; container_image only when enabled (off by default) and a changed file names an image

Budget: per new head, the PR file list (1 call per 100 files) plus 1 tarball, shared by every scanner; an already-scanned or superseded head costs nothing; a budget park writes budget_exceeded rows and the head is retried on the next delta; no model is called on a push; a PR run never sweeps, auto-resolves or stores an SBOM

X-13: GET /pulls/:n/new-findings (head.scanned, repopulse check --wait) waits for secrets, sensitive_change and the enabled always-run pattern scanners, and for dependency_cve / container_image only once they have started at that head; PR_SCANS=off removes the pattern scanners from the push and from the wait; per-repo enablement is respected

docs/CI_INTEGRATION.md states exactly what runs per PR push, what does not, and the forge cost; the Coverage table says 'on every pull request push' (or the conditional wording); PR_SCANS is in the env registry and docs/CONFIG.md

notes: Defaults chosen (cheap to change): PR scans on (PR_SCANS=on); only OPEN pull requests; at most 3 heads per delta, newest first (older heads wait for the next delta); conditional scanners run first so the CI wait sees them start before the rest finish; a scanner with nothing to read at the head still records a run (semgrep and performance a succeeded 'Nothing to scan' row) so the wait ends; a budget park is retried, any other tarball failure records failed rows; dependency file detection covers every ECOSYSTEMS lockfile plus package.json, pyproject.toml, requirements*.txt/.in, Pipfile, setup.py/cfg, go.mod, Cargo.toml, Gemfile, composer.json, pom.xml, build.gradle(.kts), *.csproj/fsproj/vbproj and the like.

FIRST SLICE 2026-10-29, acceptance 2 and 3; stays in_progress. runStoredVerdictTweakPass (packages/security/src/rules/triage-clusters.ts) reads this workspace's stored ai_triage_verdicts (30 days, newest first opinion per finding; a verdict a person dismissed, a superseded one and second opinions are left out) and runs runTriageTweakPass on them. The worker's weekly rule_draft_pass job (workspace-scoped, same AI-paused check, same workspace gateway, Tier 2) now runs it right after the dismissal drafter; combineLearningPasses writes one run row for both. A timeout or provider error on one call is recorded on the row and the next cluster still runs; failed only when every call failed. No new scanner key, no migration.

NOTHING CAN PROMOTE OR CHANGE A RULE, and a hole was closed on the way: a registry row overrides a shipped rule's status BY ID (shadow.ts effectiveStatus), so a proposal named after a live pack rule would have put that live rule back in shadow. A proposal now never takes a reserved id: the cluster's source rule, any shipped pack id (shipped-ids.ts reads the rulepack YAML), any registry row in the workspace, or any rule that has raised a finding there; a collision is counted as `collided` and nothing is written. DB test: existing live and shadow rows equal before and after (both workspaces), the one new row is status proposed with llm_draft:ai_triage provenance and no shadow start, the rulepacks tree hashes the same, findings stay open, another workspace's verdicts never reach the prompt, and a second week changes nothing. The dismissal drafter (draft-run.ts) has the same id hole and is NOT changed here.

tickets.title: Verified fixes ready by default for top confirmed findings
acceptance: After judging, verified fixes are drafted for the top confirmed findings within the time budget and listed as ready to apply
A draft that fails the rescan is recorded with its reason and never shown as a fix
notes: Planned 2026-10-28 from the owner's 'close the loop' request; design in docs/design/CLOSE_THE_LOOP.md.

2026-10-29 built (apps/api/src/workers/ai-fix.ts): drafting runs in the judge's own ai_pass_runs row right after judging, so it spends the judge's wall-clock budget (judge_minutes_per_day / AI_JUDGE_SCAN_MINUTES) with no second ledger; once a fix could be drafted the judge keeps a third of the run for it. Targets: open/confirmed findings with verify_status confirmed and a re-runnable rule (target.ts isRerunnable), riskiest first, at most 5 a run, with no answer yet at the snapshot (a rejected draft is a verdict and is not re-asked; a failed one waits 24 h). Each is the W18-19 job (runPatchDraft: draft, apply at the scanned commit, re-scan); requested_by null marks it as drafted after the scan. Local patch route: on by default; hosted patch route: only inside a judge run on the hosted opt-in (budget calls) and only to destinations that acknowledgement names; AI off stops it, checked before each draft; AI_JUDGE=off stops it with the judge. A timeout, provider or forge error on one draft is recorded on its row and on plan.fixes and the loop goes on (3 in a row stop it). The judge queues a run when nothing is left to judge but a confirmed finding still needs a fix.

Listed as ready to apply: GET /patches/ready (members; verified rows only, for the snapshot the drawer shows, on open/confirmed findings, riskiest first, workspace-filtered) and a 'Fixes ready to apply' panel on the findings page (widgets/findings/ReadyFixes.tsx) that opens the finding's drawer, where the existing Verified fix section shows the diff with Copy/Download. Write scope widened to apps/api/src/routes/patches/** (the list endpoint; auto drafts no longer count against people's 50-a-day cap) and apps/web/src/routes/findings/index.tsx (mounting the panel).

Fixed on the way (packages/security/src/patches/run.ts): drafts now route by the `patch` role (meta.role); they routed by the finding's dimension, so a patch chain an admin set was named in the drawer but not used. No migration; no new env var.
